messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 71
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Oceania
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Cashier
- Trauma Type: Witnessed other trauma
- Pcl5: 57

**Case Vignette: Mr. A. (Age 71, Male, Oceania)**

Mr. A. presents as a soft-spoken, weathered man whose hands, though still steady, tremble slightly when he removes his cap. He is a cashier at a large hardware store, a job he took after retiring from his lifelong work as a fisherman. He explains this change with a quiet, rueful smile, saying the ocean “stopped feeling like home.” He has been married to his wife, Lani, for forty-eight years.

The traumatic event that shattered his world occurred two years ago, on a Tuesday afternoon. Mr. A. was working the register near the main entrance. A young man, later identified as a teenager from a neighboring town, walked in, purchased a single energy drink, and then, without warning, produced a handgun. Mr. A. remembers the sound as a flat, dry crack—not the boom he expected from movies. He watched, frozen, as the young man raised the gun to his own head and pulled the trigger. The boy collapsed three feet from Mr. A.’s register. The store went silent for a single, terrible second, then erupted in screams.

Mr. A. did not scream. He did not move. He stood at his register, his hand still hovering over the scanner, until the police arrived. He remembers the blood spreading on the gray linoleum, a dark, glossy stain that looked like spilled oil. He was interviewed, sent home, and told to take a few days off.

Now, two years later, Mr. A. still works the same register. He requested a transfer to the back of the store, but management said his years of experience were needed at the front. He cannot refuse. The store is the only place he feels he has a purpose. Yet, every shift is a battle.

The sound of a shopping cart’s squeaky wheel makes his stomach drop. A customer dropping a heavy box on the counter sends a jolt of electricity through his spine. He has developed a compulsive habit of counting the number of people in his line, ensuring he can see everyone’s hands. He scans items, but his eyes dart, scanning, always scanning. He avoids eye contact with young men, especially those wearing hooded sweatshirts. He has memorized the exact spot on the floor where the boy fell, and he will not step on that tile. He walks around it, every time.

At home, the symptoms are worse. He cannot sit with his back to the door in a restaurant. He no longer enjoys the family gatherings that once defined his life. The sound of a car backfiring sends him to the ground, his heart hammering against his ribs. He has become a stranger to his own grandchildren, who do not understand why their grandfather flinches when they run up to hug him from behind.

His sleep is a minefield. He wakes three or four times a night, drenched in sweat, the image of the boy’s face—a face he had never seen before—burned into his mind. He has stopped watching the news. The sight of any act of violence, even in a fictional movie, triggers a pounding headache and a feeling of unreality, as if he is watching himself from across the room.

He is irritable, a fact that pains him more than anything. He snapped at Lani last week for putting a spoon in the wrong drawer. He later wept in the bathroom, ashamed. He feels a constant, low-grade dread, a sense that the world is a thin, fragile shell that can shatter at any moment. He no longer trusts the safety of a Tuesday afternoon. He carries the weight of that single, flat sound with him everywhere, a silent passenger on every shift, every meal, every quiet night. He came to therapy not because he thought it would help, but because Lani asked him to, and he cannot bear to disappoint her.
